video.title: Distributions and histograms: The shape of the data
video.format_note: Animated explainer, 16:9, flat Darsi colours on paper-grey backgrounds. Charts draw themselves; code is typed out on a card, left to right in both languages. Narration in the lesson language; captions as separate files, never burned in.
cast: Ms Amina Bello - the students' teacher (main character)
Mr Joseph - the students' maths teacher (cameo)
Narrator - the Darsi voice, talking to the student (warm, peer to peer)

scenes.narration: We measured the heights of sixty pupils for the health check. Sixty numbers in a long list. Nobody could see anything in them. So we drew their shape.
Today: how a histogram shows the shape of your data.

scenes.on_screen_text: A distribution: how values spread out
scenes.narration: A distribution tells you how often each value happens. Are most pupils near the middle height? Are there many very tall or very short pupils? That is the shape of the data.

A histogram groups the values into equal bins. Here each bin is five centimetres wide: one forty to one forty five, one forty five to one fifty, and so on. Then we count how many pupils fall in each bin.
Each bar is one bin, and its height is the count. Our bars rise to a peak in the middle and fall away on both sides, like a hill.

scenes.on_screen_text: Symmetric: a hill in the middle
scenes.narration: A shape like this is called symmetric. The two sides look alike, so the mean and the median are almost the same. Heights, shoe sizes and many test marks look like this.

Journey times look different. Most pupils live close, but a few travel for an hour. The bars bunch on the left with a long tail to the right. This is skewed right, and the tail pulls the mean above the median.
Quick check! The journey times are skewed right. Which middle describes a typical pupil better?
The median. The few long journeys pull the mean up, so the mean is longer than most pupils' journeys. The median stays with the typical pupil.
In the app, open Build a histogram. Change the bin width from one to twenty. Too few bins hide the hill, and too many make a jagged comb.
Your turn. In a histogram of test marks, what does the height of each bar show?
How many pupils got marks in that bin. Remember: equal bins, bars that count, and a shape that is symmetric or skewed. The shape tells you which middle to trust.
Try it yourself: measure the hand spans of your family or friends, and put them in equal bins. Draw the histogram and ask: is it a hill, or does it have a tail?

checkpoints.prompt: The journey times are skewed right. Which middle describes a typical pupil better?
checkpoints.feedback_correct: Correct: the long tail pulls the mean up, but not the median.
checkpoints.feedback_wrong: Not quite: in skewed data the tail pulls the mean. The median stays typical.

checkpoints.prompt: In a histogram of test marks, what does the height of each bar show?

options.text: How many pupils have marks in that bin

checkpoints.feedback_correct: Correct: each bar counts the values that fall in its bin.
checkpoints.feedback_wrong: Not quite: a bar's height is a count, the number of values in that bin.
